title: Understanding Grease Build-Up in Kitchen P-Traps
description: Liquid cooking oils and melted fats may flow smoothly down the sink while hot, but as they hit cold standing water in the P-trap and uninsulated drain lines, they cool and solidify. Over time, this fat layer coats the inner pipe walls, capturing micro food particles and gradually restricting wastewater flow. Chemical cleaners often fail to break down thick grease coats entirely and can damage pipe seals if misused. To maintain proper kitchen drainage, wipe greasy cookware with paper towels before washing, and periodically run hot tap water down the drain to keep light residues moving.

Clean soft daylighting, realistic plastic textures, accurate slip-nut compression fittings, and true-to-life pipe geometry. No text, no logos, no watermarks, no artificial symbols.
visual_story: The visual provides a clear, realistic cross-section cutaway of a kitchen P-trap beneath a sink. Viewers can immediately notice how liquid fat hardens along the lower bend of the trap and horizontal arm, physically constricting the interior diameter of the pipe. This illustrates why kitchen sinks slow down over time even when large food scraps are avoided.

on_image_text.explanation: Warm fats solidify as they cool inside the trap, coating pipe walls and narrowing the drainage path.
on_image_text.takeaway: Scrape fats into trash containers before washing cookware; keep grease out of the drainage line.
